Nvidia is giving King Yuan Electronics (2449.TW), known as KYEC, a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to build new U.S. chip-testing facilities, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027. KYEC was one of six supplier plans in the same release. “Capacity is the constraint,” CEO Jensen Huang said in it. The bigger figure sits in Nvidia’s Q2 fiscal 2027 10-Q. Supply and capacity commitments jumped to $279 billion as of July 26, from $119 billion a quarter earlier, primarily for memory and manufacturing facilities. The KYEC advance is about 0.4% of that. What Wednesday’s deals show is where the money is going: the slow steps between a finished chip design and a shipped system. That stretch has already slipped once this year, when Nvidia’s Kyber rack design was reportedly pushed from 2027 to 2028 over a circuit-board manufacturing problem. The filing schedules $87 billion of those commitments for fiscal 2028 and $88 billion for fiscal 2029. The Street expects revenue of $692 billion in fiscal 2028, up 68% from the $412 billion expected this year, and $903 billion in fiscal 2029. On those estimates, the commitments equal about 13% of fiscal 2028 revenue and 10% of fiscal 2029. title: NVDA Stock Rebounds Above $220 as Amazon Buys Billions in Nvidia Chips but Electricity Constraints Threaten Returns - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares have rebounded above $220 after falling from a record $243, but data-center power shortages, rising financing costs, semiconductor supply constraints and growing competition threaten the sustainability of the rally. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares recovered above $220 after retreating toward $212 last Friday, reversing part of their decline from a record above $243 earlier this month. The rebound reflects improving semiconductor sentiment, supported by expectations that memory shortages and higher prices could persist through 2027. However, the recovery comes amid growing concerns about the cost of expanding computing infrastructure. Investors are questioning whether technology companies can generate sufficient returns from their enormous investments, particularly as borrowing costs rise and competition intensifies. Although Nvidia remains a leading supplier of advanced processors, the latest developments highlight the financial and operational challenges facing its customers. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) is reportedly purchasing billions of dollars in Nvidia hardware, but some server racks are sitting in warehouses because data centers lack sufficient electricity to operate them, according to Business Insider. Internal emails reportedly indicated that Amazon expected to receive $5 billion in Nvidia server systems in August, followed by another $3 billion per month. The company also introduced an “Early Rack Receipt” program, allowing it to secure equipment before facilities are ready to use it. Previously, Amazon generally waited until hardware arrived at its data centers before taking ownership. The revised approach allows it to secure scarce equipment earlier, but also exposes the company to storage costs and delays between delivery and deployment. The situation illustrates a key risk for Nvidia: strong orders do not necessarily translate into immediate revenue generation for customers. If power shortages delay installations, returns on infrastructure investments could take longer to materialise, potentially affecting future spending decisions. Expectations for higher memory prices have provided some support to semiconductor shares. Dell CEO Michael Dell reportedly warned that memory shortages could worsen in 2027, while analysts at Mizuho and KeyBanc have highlighted the potential for NAND flash prices to increase as infrastructure demand expands. Higher memory prices could benefit manufacturers across the supply chain, although they may also increase the cost of building and operating computing systems. For Nvidia, the key question is whether customers can continue expanding their infrastructure budgets while absorbing higher costs for memory, processors, electricity and data-center construction. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive a below $213 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement this week. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that semiconductor manufacturing capacity planned for 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy expected demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Despite these strong figures, its U.S.-listed shares reportedly fell around 4%, adding pressure to Nvidia and AMD. The warning highlights the difficulty of expanding production quickly enough to meet demand. Supply constraints could support semiconductor pricing, but they may also delay the delivery of equipment needed to sustain industry growth. Financing concerns have intensified following heavy selling in CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV). Yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly reached 15% before closing around 14.5%, reflecting significant investor concern about credit risk. Such borrowing costs raise questions about the sustainability of debt-financed data-center expansion. If infrastructure operators face increasingly expensive financing, some projects could be delayed or scaled back, weakening future demand for Nvidia processors. Reports of potential large financing arrangements involving SpaceX and Nvidia GPUs, alongside Amazon’s exploration of chip-financing structures, further illustrate the capital required to maintain the expansion. Microsoft’s Maia 300 processor adds another competitive threat. The chip reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while a 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor. Custom silicon could help cloud providers improve efficiency and reduce dependence on external suppliers for selected workloads. Nvidia’s established ecosystem remains a major advantage, but increasing competition could eventually pressure its pricing power and market share in certain applications. Questions surrounding OpenAI’s revenue have also renewed scrutiny of technology-sector spending assumptions. Its annualised revenue run rate was reportedly around $50 billion at the end of September, below the widely circulated $68 billion figure, which reportedly included revenue generated by partners. Nvidia is also reportedly considering further investment in Reflection AI, although discussions have not resulted in a confirmed agreement. These developments highlight how investor sentiment increasingly depends on whether substantial infrastructure investments can be supported by sustainable commercial demand. Nvidia’s rebound above $220 offers some relief after its retreat from $243, but the recovery remains vulnerable to renewed selling. Memory demand and continued semiconductor investment provide support, while power shortages, expensive financing and custom-chip competition complicate the outlook. A sustained recovery will require buyers to regain confidence that infrastructure spending can deliver sufficient returns. Until then, elevated valuations leave Nvidia exposed to further profit-taking if customers delay projects or expectations for future demand weaken.

An interest rate increase could cause some companies to borrow less to build out AI infrastructure due to higher interest costs, slowing overall progress. That's the prevailing line of thinking in the market right now, but it's extremely short-sighted. While an interest rate hike could be coming, the reality is that nothing is stopping the AI build-out. Many AI hyperscalers plan years in advance for how they will spend their money, and as long as there is still massive demand for new AI technology (and there is), this space will be a great one to invest in. With the market selling off pretty much every stock associated with AI, now is the perfect time to swoop in and buy these stocks at a discount. Nvidia makes GPUs, while Broadcom partners directly with AI hyperscalers to design custom AI computing units optimized for the workloads they will run. Many companies are choosing between a hybrid approach of Nvidia GPUs and custom AI chips, and there is plenty of growth to go around. As long as the AI market stays healthy, Micron's stock will be a must-own in 2027. title: Why Nvidia stock is rising on Wednesday? - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA shares climbed 2.44% on Wednesday at around 1:20 PM EST after the chipmaker unveiled a new reference design intended to speed up the construction of AI data centers, as the company looks to address infrastructure constraints that have slowed the expansion of computing capacity. The stock's advance came amid a broader recovery in chipmakers following last week's weakness. All three major US indexes traded higher, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gaining more than 1%. At its GTC Berlin 2026 conference, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang presented the company's DSX POD AI Factory reference design, which aims to reduce the time required to deploy AI infrastructure from months to weeks. Building large data centers has become a major challenge for the AI industry, with companies racing to add capacity to support growing demand for computing power. Nvidia's latest design seeks to accelerate that process by bringing factory-built precision and speed to infrastructure deployment. The DSX POD is approximately the size of a standard shipping container and weighs around 28,000 kilograms, or nearly 62,000 pounds, Nvidia said. “An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete." “With NVIDIA DSX POD, we’re bringing factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure construction — reducing deployment time from months to weeks so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online faster.” The announcement highlights Nvidia's growing focus on the infrastructure surrounding its chips, as faster deployment could help customers begin generating returns from AI investments sooner. Nvidia also signed a joint declaration with Germany to advance industrial AI and strengthen cooperation through the Industry 4.0 Platform, alongside partners such as Siemens. The company announced support for German startups Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. The investments form part of a broader commitment to developing a European AI ecosystem valued at nearly $10 billion. Nvidia also introduced its OpenShell Reference Architecture as it works to strengthen safeguards for AI agents. Separately, it announced a humanoid robot reference design in collaboration with Agile Robots, extending its push into robotics and industrial applications. Demand from China remained another focus, with ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent having reportedly ordered more than 3 million Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards. The orders carry a combined potential value exceeding $35 billion. The reported purchases underscore continued demand for Nvidia hardware among major Chinese technology companies despite Washington's restrictions on shipments of advanced AI chips. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs reiterated its Buy rating on Nvidia and maintained its $300 price target following the Berlin event. The investment bank said Nvidia's announcements reinforced its assessment that AI deployments remain on track for the foreseeable future, while cautioning that the developments might not translate into an immediate move in the stock. Shenzhen-listed Tansun Technology disclosed on October 13 a deal for 20,000 of the cards from an unidentified seller. One source said partners might receive only 5% to 10% of what they requested. Nvidia indicated it can produce no more than 3 million of these cards globally in 2027, well below Chinese orders alone. The constraint is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) capacity, much of which Nvidia is expected to commit to Rubin in 2027. TSMC declined to comment. Management said its revenue opportunity rises from $25 billion with Blackwell to $40 billion with Vera Rubin per gigawatt. It already called its projected fiscal 2028 growth of approximately 70% a “supply-constrained outlook.” Even a partial fill would be small against Data Center revenue of $89.02 billion in a single quarter. The orders signal pricing power and a backlog. They come in a market many investors had dismissed, and the expansion that creates that backlog has to be powered and cooled by somebody (we covered seven of those suppliers in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade). An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese workstation chipmakers have seen “unprecedented growth since 2022” because U.S. firms face “outdated US export controls” and Chinese import limits. Nvidia wants looser rules, so that statement is advocacy. Beijing recently proposed its own export controls on AI technologies, and Taiwan plans to outlaw unauthorized AI chip exports, while ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and China’s industry ministry did not respond to requests for comment. Rubin drives the investment case more than China does. These orders sit entirely outside guidance, so any shipped volume is upside to a business that just reported quarterly revenue of $96.22 billion, up 105.8% year over year. At roughly 44 times earnings, the stock trades at a premium valuation, though the recent pullback reduces it slightly. The test is the earnings report expected on November 18, a date Nvidia has not confirmed. If management puts China compute revenue into guidance or confirms RTX PRO 5500 volumes, the story moves from reported to booked, and if it stays silent, these orders remain a demand signal only. It weighs about 62,000 pounds and can ship by truck on normal roads. The cabling and liquid cooling are all built at the factory. When it arrives, it just needs to be placed, connected to other containers, and tested. Nvidia says this cuts the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days. The launch fits a bigger trend as Nvidia’s systems started as single chips, growing into servers, then full racks, and now a ready-made pod. title: Nvidia Stock Gains. Its European Partnerships Could Open New Growth Market - TradingView
content: NVIDIA NVDA shares rose about 2% early Wednesday as the chipmaker expanded its autonomous-driving business through new and expanded partnerships with European automakers and mobility companies, according to a Wednesday press release. The agreements span passenger cars, robotaxis and commercial transport, extending NVIDIA's role beyond supplying chips to providing computing systems and software for self-driving vehicles. Bolt plans to use NVIDIA technology with future Lucid vehicles for a European robotaxi service, targeting a fleet of at least 25,000 vehicles over time. Volvo Cars is adopting NVIDIA's Hyperion platform, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack for automated driving. Mercedes-Benz is extending its collaboration with NVIDIA on Level 3 and Level 4 capabilities, while Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles has showcased an autonomous ID. Buzz platform. NVIDIA also introduced Halos SAFE, a framework that combines simulated driving scenarios with physical testing to assess vehicle safety. Its Alpamayo 2 Edge model is designed for in-car computing systems to interpret driving scenes and plan vehicle movements. Bolt expects to begin collecting real-world driving data in Madrid in 2027, subject to regulatory approval, with Germany a priority for future expansion. The investment value of this "full-stack AI" strategy lies in linking demand expansion, accelerated delivery, and improved power efficiency. This creates conditions for NVIDIA to diversify revenue streams and for clients to enhance investment returns, while also providing new fundamental support for the semiconductor rebound to evolve into an earnings-driven rally. As NVIDIA (NVDA.US) held its highly anticipated GTC conference in Berlin, AI computing power themes and global technology stocks experienced volatile recovery and consolidation following a sharp decline. For the week ending October 16, the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 5.49%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, regarded as the bellwether for "AI computing power trades," dropped approximately 11.41%. Micron and SanDisk plunged 14.59% and 17.86% respectively, making memory chips the hardest-hit sector in this correction. South Korea's KOSPI Index sank 14.46% over the same period, marking its largest weekly decline since October 2008. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell approximately 17.8% and 24.3% respectively, indicating that the AI sell-off has transmitted across markets along the AI computing hardware supply chain. On October 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rebounded 1.61%, ending an eight-day losing streak, while the Nasdaq 100 Index rose 1.17%; Micron and SanDisk gained 2.97% and 5.53% respectively. However, on the 20th, both indices retreated by 0.29% and 0.13% respectively, with memory stocks also giving up some gains. On the 21st, the South Korean stock market strengthened again, with the KOSPI rising 3.29% to 5,735.66 points; Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix climbed 5.67% and 5.81% respectively. Recent market movements highlight the emergence of bottom-fishing capital closely tracking AI computing themes and the broader semiconductor sector, though sustained revaluation still requires evidence from earnings and investment returns. Against this backdrop, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang sent positive signals at the Berlin GTC conference, urging Europe to accelerate the implementation of AI applications. He pointed out that for Europe to truly establish an AI ecosystem and AI economy, end-user industries such as automotive, financial services, and healthcare must accelerate AI adoption and transform into AI-driven enterprises. For the technology sector, which is facing skepticism regarding AI investment returns, this statement shifts market focus from infrastructure construction to end-user demand: only when AI continuously integrates into corporate operations, industrial production, and professional service processes will early investments in computing power have the opportunity to translate into sustainable commercial revenue. Capital flow data disclosed by Wall Street financial giant JPMorgan on October 19 echoed market trends. For the week ending October 16, global equity ETFs saw inflows of $46.3 billion. Among them, SOXL (a triple-leveraged bullish ETF tracking the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, ticker: "SOXL") recorded a record single-week inflow of $7.2 billion. ETF products tracking South Korea saw cumulative significant inflows of $1.3 billion, the strongest since July, with approximately $600 million flowing into the triple-leveraged bullish Korea ETF, KORU. Meanwhile, DRAM-themed ETFs experienced redemptions for the eighth consecutive week, with latest single-week outflows totaling $900 million. These capital dynamics highlight that while the market is actively betting on a semiconductor rebound, bullish confidence in valuation and earnings expansion cycles for the semiconductor sector, including the memory chip supply chain, has not yet synchronized with the recovery, reflecting a coexistence of leveraged bottom-fishing and institutional risk reduction. Zhitong Finance APP learns that NVIDIA's core response to the global technology sell-off at the Berlin GTC conference was to further ground the AI growth narrative in faster delivery speeds for AI GPU computing clusters, higher output per unit of electricity, and the continuous expansion of AI application coverage driven by AI agents. Jensen Huang divided the AI industry into five layers: energy, computing power, AI factories, models, and applications, stating that the new generation of AI computing clusters based on the Vera Rubin architecture has entered full-scale production. During this European tour, he committed to investing nearly $10 billion in the local technology ecosystem, with a cooperation network exceeding 12,000 partners. These deployments indicate that NVIDIA is simultaneously expanding infrastructure supply and downstream usage scenarios, aiming to convert Europe's industrial knowledge, corporate data, and sovereign AI demands into broader computing expenditure. Based on a unified benchmark of the closing price of $216.47 on October 20, S&P Global statistics displayed by StockAnalysis cover 62 senior Wall Street analysts. Their average 12-month target price for NVIDIA is $328.72, implying a potential upside of 51.85%, with a consensus rating of "Strong Buy." The highest target price in the aforementioned statistics comes from Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold, who set a target of $515, which is 137.91% higher than $216.47. He reiterated this judgment in a recent interview with Bloomberg. His model projects that fiscal year revenue could approach $1 trillion by January 2029, valued at approximately 22 times calendar year 2028 earnings, corresponding to earnings per share of about $23.41. Key supports for this judgment include improved supply releasing delivery capacity, system revenue expansion from Rubin and Vera, and customer growth in enterprise, sovereign AI, and professional cloud sectors. Therefore, this most optimistic target price is primarily built on significantly higher earnings forecasts. The production expansion agreements, modular deployment, and industrial application expansion conveyed at the Berlin GTC correspond to key links in whether these forecasts can be realized. However, the target price still depends on whether assumptions regarding revenue growth, profit margins, and valuations are met, and does not imply that the stock price will inevitably reach that level. From 14-day deployment to large-scale supply chain expansion: Striving to shorten the distance between computing power and actual cash flow As semiconductor and memory stocks experience sharp declines and the market reassesses AI investment returns, NVIDIA's Berlin GTC provides a more concrete path for realizing the AI growth narrative—DSX POD compresses on-site deployment time after infrastructure readiness to as fast as 14 days, enabling earlier operationalization of computing power; the OpenShell security architecture collaborates with Vera and Rubin platforms to support agents delving into corporate business, thereby broadening computing demand through applications in industrial manufacturing, telecommunications networks, and robotics. Meanwhile, capacity expansion in substrates, advanced packaging, testing, and optical interconnects provides support for subsequent system deliveries. The investment value of the complete "full-stack AI" layout recently spearheaded by NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang lies in connecting demand expansion, accelerated delivery, and increased output per unit of electricity. This creates conditions for NVIDIA to continue accelerating the expansion of revenue sources and improving customer investment returns. It also provides new fundamental basis for the semiconductor sector and broader technology stocks to sustain a major rebound into a new bull market phase driven by earnings, suggesting that NVIDIA's stock price hitting $500 may only be a matter of time. The DSX POD is a Modular AI Factory Reference Design based on the Vera Rubin platform, unveiled by NVIDIA at GTC Berlin. Partners pre-integrate computing, networking, rack power distribution, and liquid cooling systems into modular containers, which are tested before being shipped to the site. NVIDIA states that, provided site power, cooling, and networking are ready, on-site deployment time can be reduced from six months to as little as 14 days. The core value lies in minimizing installation and commissioning time, allowing compute resources to begin training and inference services—and generating revenue—sooner. Jensen Huang indicated that deliveries of these systems are scheduled to begin in early 2027. The most direct value of the DSX POD, recently disclosed at GTC Berlin, is compressing the time between equipment delivery and formal operations. This Vera Rubin-based Modular AI Factory Reference Design shifts the integration and validation of computing, networking, cabling, rack power, and liquid cooling to the manufacturing facility. Consequently, for sites where power, cooling, and networking are already prepared, on-site deployment time is reduced from six months to as fast as 14 days. Partners including Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv plan to begin deliveries in early 2027. This modular design is particularly suitable for smaller-scale deployments under 1 gigawatt. Its economic significance lies in enabling parallel execution of equipment integration and site preparation, reducing on-site rework and commissioning, and allowing invested capital to generate billable services earlier. Regarding operating costs, NVIDIA estimates that DSX MaxLPS can reduce power consumption by up to 30% for the same token output through dynamic allocation of power budgets. Closed-loop liquid cooling combined with dry coolers can bring facility water usage for cooling close to zero, saving up to 54 million liters of water per day compared to traditional cooling towers at a 2-gigawatt scale. DSX Flex further coordinates computing loads with grid supply and demand, while DSX OS and SimReady tools cover infrastructure management and simulation. This combination shifts the competitive focus to how much effective computing can be delivered under given power access conditions and what level of operating costs must be borne. More specific deployment paths have emerged on the customer side: Google Cloud plans to commercially launch its A5X instances powered by Vera Rubin NVL72 in November, followed by expansion into Europe, with plans to deploy up to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. In Europe, Nscale is advancing Vera Rubin infrastructure, NEBIUS combines Groq 3 LPX with Rubin and Spectrum-X for low-latency inference, and Mistral plans to receive Rubin systems in 2027. These developments connect large model training, reinforcement learning, and agent inference to actual cloud service products. To support delivery, NVIDIA is simultaneously driving capacity expansion among key suppliers through capacity reservation agreements and advance payments. Three agreements with IBIDEN, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron correspond to a target of expanding advanced substrate production capacity by 2.5 times over the next three years: IBIDEN received billions of dollars in advance payments, aiming to triple the capacity of its Ono factory in Japan, with new capacity ramp-up starting in Q1 2028; Samsung Electro-Mechanics has joined the supply chain, providing existing capacity in Korea and advancing expansions in Sejong and Busan; Unimicron’s KF project is expected to increase supply in Q2 2027 and potentially reach full production by mid-2028. Other bottlenecks are being alleviated concurrently: Amkor plans to increase its interposer wafer capacity in Korea by more than 300% by the end of 2028; NVIDIA’s total testing capacity is planned to double between 2026 and 2027, with an $1.1 billion advance payment to King Yuan Electronics supporting mass production at U.S. testing facilities in April 2027, while Singapore expansion is expected to reach mass production in February of the same year; Siliconware’s co-packaged optics (CPO) optical engine capacity targets a 15-fold expansion by mid-2027 and another doubling by the end of 2028. For investors, these commitments improve the visibility of medium-term orders for relevant suppliers and help NVIDIA convert chip output into complete system deliveries. Benefits in the memory segment are primarily reflected through HBM adoption demand and server memory and storage expansion, with specific profit elasticity depending on supply, demand, and pricing for each category. From the surge in AI agents at tech companies to telecom operator base stations: NVIDIA strives to embed AI computing resource demands into more industries. The focus of this OpenShell upgrade is extending the agent secure runtime into a complete infrastructure architecture. Here, Rubin handles model inference, the Vera CPU manages tool calls, code execution, and task orchestration, and the BlueField-4 data processing unit runs Sentry to continuously monitor behavior and enforce hardware-level policies, isolating out-of-bounds agents within milliseconds. NVIDIA claims Sentry can increase agent hosting capacity by up to 20%; the statement that Rubin offers “up to 30 times the throughput per megawatt of GB300” is based on specific AgentX workloads and interaction speed conditions. Its commercial value lies in simultaneously expanding computing power and controllable execution capabilities, enabling enterprises to deploy more agents with actual permissions into production processes. The accompanying Agent Toolkit adds the Agent Knowledge Foundation: Nemotron Retriever handles document parsing, retrieval, and reranking; Kumo performs prediction and anomaly detection for relational tables, spreadsheets, and time series; and Auto-Ontology maps raw data to business entities such as customers, products, and orders. Companies like Palantir, Databricks, Snowflake, and SAP are participating in related applications; the newly added Confidential Bare Metal protects models and data running on third-party infrastructure. It follows that as agents penetrate deeper into enterprise operations, demand will extend to CPUs, data processing, runtime environments, and security infrastructure, thereby increasing the share of enterprise computing budgets that NVIDIA can capture. Open model portfolios serve to expand application entry points: Nemotron 3.5 covers language and vision tasks, Cosmos 3.5 supports physical world modeling and synthetic data generation, Alpamayo 2 Edge targets vehicle-side scene understanding and motion planning, BioNeMo RFD4-Proteina is used for protein design, and Ising serves quantum hardware calibration and error correction. Enterprises can customize these models using local data and deploy them on infrastructure under their own control. For NVIDIA, open models lower the barrier to industry application development and create more usage scenarios for CUDA, inference software, and hardware platforms. Telecommunications networks are providing new entry points for distributed computing power. T-Mobile has completed its first AI-RAN call on a commercial network, while Elisa enabled voice, mobile data, and visual AI to run on the same acceleration platform during live trials in Europe. BT and Deutsche Telekom plan to advance live network trials by 2027, and nine operators across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa are building or expanding related infrastructure. Jensen Huang’s statement at the Berlin GTC that “all carriers will provide AI computing power” refers to leveraging existing sites, power supplies, fiber optics, and geographic coverage to deploy certain inference services closer to users and machines. By sharing platforms for wireless access processing and AI applications, carriers have the opportunity to increase revenue from computing services, while NVIDIA gains deployment space beyond central data centers. In the manufacturing sector, the FOX factory operations blueprint, currently in early access, integrates equipment logs, visual inspection, production planning, and digital twins with AI agents. Siemens reported that calibration time for related inspections at its Erlangen factory was reduced by 40%. The commercially available cuDSS sparse linear solver accelerates engineering simulations, with Synopsys software achieving up to 40x and 12x speedups in specific tests for imec lithography models and Infineon device simulations, respectively. Such applications directly link computing expenditures to R&D cycles, production efficiency, and quality costs, providing measurable justification for industrial customers to expand their AI budgets. Collaborations in the automotive industry further illustrate NVIDIA’s strategy to extend AI from data centers into the real economy. In addition to Volvo using Hyperion and Alpamayo to develop autonomous vehicles, and Bolt planning to deploy at least 25,000 future Lucid models with L4 capabilities based on Hyperion in Europe, Volkswagen is also employing NVIDIA technology in the commercial vehicle sector. These partnerships connect on-board computing, autonomous driving software, simulation training, and cloud infrastructure, opening up more application scenarios for AI computing demand. In the realm of Physical AI, the Isaac platform has added runtime environments, training frameworks, and data workflows. Agile Robots plans to launch the Agile ONE SN research humanoid robot platform, based on Jetson Thor and GR00T, in early 2027. NVIDIA also stated that the Physical AI market generated approximately $11 billion in revenue in the first half of this year, with growth rates reaching up to 30%. This figure reflects the commercial potential of real-world AI applications such as robotics, though specific year-on-year benchmarks and revenue accounting methods require verification against the company’s original disclosures. In the healthcare sector, NVIDIA and Siemens Healthineers are advancing adaptive radiotherapy by dynamically adjusting radiation doses based on patient breathing and body movement, while connecting protein design with experimental processes via BioNeMo. These initiatives drive demand for cloud-based training, simulation validation, and edge inference. Local computing is also part of this landscape: RTX Spark Windows laptops, which began listing last week, bring Blackwell RTX GPUs, up to 128GB of unified memory, and AI software to personal devices, complementing DGX Spark and DGX Station to cover developer and enterprise use cases. This product portfolio, spanning from the cloud to the network edge and end devices, enables NVIDIA to support agent deployments under varying requirements for cost, latency, and data control. Overall, the signals from the Berlin GTC indicate that NVIDIA is not merely launching new generations of chips and AI systems, but is attempting to simultaneously address issues regarding the delivery efficiency of AI infrastructure, energy consumption, supply chain bottlenecks, and the implementation of end-user applications. Modular deployment is expected to shorten the time required to operationalize computing investments, while expansions in substrates, packaging, testing, and optical interconnects provide support for system delivery. Scenarios such as enterprise agents, industrial manufacturing, telecommunications networks, robotics, and automotive further expand potential demand. For markets reassessing AI return on investment, these developments offer new fundamental indicators; however, whether they can sustain a new round of continuous growth ultimately depends on whether infrastructure investments translate into genuine revenue, whether customers achieve measurable returns, and whether NVIDIA’s own profit growth meets market expectations. title: The AI Buildout Is Only 15% Complete—Here Is Where the Next Dollar Actually Goes - MarketBeat
content:
AI stocks are selling off, and the reflex is to treat that as the market finally pricing in reality. Dan Ives, the longtime technology analyst who left Wedbush to launch Yorkville Ives, reads it the other way. By his estimate, less than 15% of total AI spending has actually happened. That number changes the question from whether the buildout pays off to which layer of it gets funded next, and that is a far more useful thing to be arguing about while the tape is red. Ives describes the AI cycle as a party that started around 9:30 p.m. and is now closer to 11:30 p.m. More companies keep getting let into the club. It is no longer just NVIDIA NASDAQ: NVDA and Jensen Huang holding the door. Advanced Micro Devices NASDAQ: AMD, Palantir Technologies NASDAQ: PLTR and Snowflake NYSE: SNOW are all inside now, and his view is that the night will run for several more hours. That does not mean a smooth ride. Macro shocks, geopolitics, circular financing arrangements and capital expenditures (CapEx) are all live sources of white-knuckle moments. The argument is about duration, not comfort. Technology has always moved faster than the rules written to govern it, and this cycle is no exception. Guardrails are coming, mostly in the form of self-regulation. The more interesting market read is competitive rather than moral. For the first time in roughly three decades, the United States appears to be ahead of China on the technology frontier, and a deliberate slowdown here does not come with a matching slowdown there. There is also a positioning game inside the safety conversation. If the leading labs agree to throttle, the companies already at the top preserve their lead while everyone behind them stalls. Call it regulatory capture with better branding. Meta Platforms NASDAQ: META could accelerate into exactly that kind of pause. The safety story is not only a risk line, it is a revenue line. Cybersecurity stocks have already shown what happens when enterprises decide protection is non-negotiable. Sovereign AI is the next version of that idea: companies want their data working for them without handing it wholesale to the model builders. Palantir has been selling that message for years, and NVIDIA has leaned into it too. One company’s constraint keeps turning into another company’s contract. Meta’s Muse assistant matters less as a product launch than as a monetization lever across roughly 3.5 billion users. Convert even a slice of that through advertising or commerce, and the math on Meta’s spending changes. The friction is already showing: Amazon blocked Muse from its store in September, which is a preview of how hard platforms will fight over whose agent touches the customer. Microsoft NASDAQ: MSFT took a bruise on Copilot share, but Azure is the line that actually matters as enterprises migrate workloads. And Apple NASDAQ: AAPL, now under new CEO John Ternus, has 1.5 billion iPhones and roughly 2.5 billion iOS devices to work with. Being late is survivable with an install base like that. The 2027 anniversary iPhone is where Ternus gets judged. Nebius Group NASDAQ: NBIS and CoreWeave NASDAQ: CRWV are spending like hyperscalers without hyperscaler balance sheets, and both posted quarters that looked like inflection points. The multiplier is the reason to care: roughly $10 of surrounding spend follows every dollar that goes into an NVIDIA chip. Power, cooling, networking, and eventually quantum work at International Business Machines NYSE: IBM all sit downstream of that. Tesla NASDAQ: TSLA is stuck between two identities, and the robotaxi ramp has run slower than hoped. The next six to nine months are a prove-it window. Ives puts better than 80% odds on a Tesla merger with Space Exploration Technologies NASDAQ: SPCX by the end of 2027, built on the idea that the combined data is worth more than either piece alone. Worth noting independently: SPCX only listed in June, staggered lockups run into December, and other analysts covering the idea have called the timing uncertain. Software is the messier group. Salesforce NYSE: CRM has an important stretch ahead to show customers are buying its AI story rather than building around it, while Adobe NASDAQ: ADBE and Intuit NASDAQ: INTU face harder structural questions. The monetization signal finally showed up last quarter at Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon. Watch whether it widens into financial services, government and healthcare budgets, because that is what turns a spending cycle into an earnings cycle. title: Nvidia GTC Berlin Keynote: Jensen Huang Puts $50 Billion Price Tag On 1GW AI Factory Amid DSX POD Launch - TradingView
content: Nvidia (NVDA) shares rose in early morning trade on Wednesday after CEO Jensen Huang unveiled DSX POD, a new system designed to get AI data centers up and running faster. Huang said a 1-gigawatt facility costs about $50 billion, making delays costly for operators. Such a facility can generate about $40 billion in annual revenue, he said, meaning a three-month delay could push back roughly $10 billion in revenue. “10 billion worth of revenues will make anybody anxious,” Huang said. DSX POD is Nvidia’s latest effort to speed up the deployment of AI computing infrastructure by shifting more assembly and testing from construction sites to the supply chain. Nvidia says the approach can cut deployment time at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days. Units are expected to be available in early 2027. NVDA stock rose as much as 2% in pre-market trade and was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around the AI bellwether shifted to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ territory over the past day. Huang said the system builds on Nvidia’s earlier move to assemble its NVLink 72 rack-scale computers within the supply chain rather than on-site. DSX POD extends that approach to a larger system, integrating computing, networking, storage, software, power and cooling into a single AI factory reference design. “Great chips alone don’t make a great AI factory,” Huang said. “NVIDIA DSX has a full-stack AI factory reference architecture, co-innovated with the world’s leading infrastructure companies.” The aim is to reduce the work required after equipment arrives at a data center, when computing capacity may remain idle while systems are assembled, connected and tested. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle capex will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable.” Huang said moving more of that work upstream could reduce the time between the arrival of computing equipment and the start of token production, when AI systems begin generating output that customers can use or pay for. “We think something along the lines of four to five months, down to about a month,” he said. Huang’s $50 billion estimate for a 1-gigawatt facility includes land, power, the building shell, computing equipment, networking, storage, power systems and cooling. The scale of that investment is particularly important for companies financing expansion with debt. CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and IREN (IREN) are among the companies building out AI computing capacity. However, the industry’s spending plans are unfolding alongside rising concerns about financing costs and the time required to turn capital spending into revenue. CoreWeave’s bond yields approached 15% last week, while CRWV stock dropped below the $60 mark in morning trade on Tuesday before recovering. CRWV stock and NBIS stock were up around 2% each in pre-market trade, while IREN stock gained more than 3%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around all three neoclouds was trending in ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past day. Nvidia is working with a broad group of technology and infrastructure companies on the design, including Dell Technologies (DELL), Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), Lenovo, Vertiv (VRT), Schneider Electric, Eaton (ETN), Pegatron, Wistron, Foxconn, Crusoe and DayOne. Nvidia supplies the reference architecture, while its partners build the systems. Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year. The DSX POD rollout adds to the company’s efforts to expand AI infrastructure in the region, with the broader goal of helping customers bring computing capacity online sooner and generate returns on their investments faster. President Donald Trump on Wednesday urged companies building artificial intelligence (AI) data centers to pay local communities or individual residents a “dividend” to secure support for new projects. In a Truth Social post, Trump said previously unpopular projects had gained support after companies reached financial agreements with communities. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!” Trump wrote. Trump also said large new data centers must generate their own electricity and supply or sell excess power to the grid, potentially lowering electricity costs. He did not specify how the dividend payments would work. Rapid AI infrastructure expansion has become a political flashpoint as communities question how energy-intensive facilities affect electricity bills, water supplies, and local infrastructure. The U.S. Department of Energy estimated that data centers could account for 6.7% to 12% of national electricity consumption by 2028, compared with 4.4% in 2023. A July report from Carbon Direct found that community opposition had delayed, withdrawn, or stalled at least 46 projects across 20 states, representing $170 billion in announced investments. In a recent TIME interview, Trump acknowledged concerns about data centers being built near homes. “It doesn't mean I want them right next to my house, but certainly I like them in my county,” he said. The president also argued that the facilities would bring economic benefits, saying, “They're going to lower your taxes.” At an October 3 rally in Ohio, he defended data-center development, warning that investments could shift to China if the U.S. blocked projects. In March, Amazon, Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle (ORCL) and xAI signed the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, agreeing to cover additional power generation and infrastructure costs associated with their facilities. Trump’s proposal to pay local communities a dividend for hosting AI data centers is “not crazy to consider,” according to Nebius Group N.V. (NBIS) Chief Revenue Officer Marc Boroditsky, who told CNBC that the company was “100% in principle” open to discussions about investing in local communities. Boroditsky said community benefits could extend beyond existing tax revenues to education, job development and direct economic opportunities. Investor Shay Boloor, in an X post, highlighted that the proposal could favor technology giants such as Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Meta (META). Boloor said paying residents and developing on-site power generation could prove far cheaper for these companies than delaying billions of dollars in AI infrastructure investments for another year. SpaceX stock traded 10% higher in Wednesday’s premarket. If the levels hold, the stock will mark its best day since August. Morningstar equity analyst Nicolas Owens said SpaceX has built a strong position in the space industry through lower launch costs and the ability to reuse rockets. The company accounted for 83% of the mass sent into orbit worldwide in 2025, nearly 10 times what its closest competitor launched, according to the analyst. Its high launch volume also helps reduce average costs and gives it an advantage over rivals such as Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. Owens added that the company’s Starlink satellite internet service benefits from this launch infrastructure. With more than 10,000 satellites in orbit, Starlink can deploy additional capacity at an internal cost that is difficult for competitors relying on outside launch providers to match. Owens estimates that SpaceX’s launch and connectivity operations generate returns on invested capital in the mid-20% range, comfortably exceeding its estimated 9.3% cost of capital. According to the analyst, SpaceX is exploring orbital data centers that could use solar power in space to reduce electricity expenses and cooling requirements. The concept relies on Starship, which is designed to carry larger payloads than the company’s existing Falcon rockets. “AI is growing so much faster than the company that we expect it to represent a majority of revenue by the end of 2026,” said Owens. However, he said engineers must still provide clarity on radiation protection, heat management, and the availability of enough bandwidth to pass data between satellites and Earth. The analyst sees cost advantage in AI computing for SpaceX, but does not yet assign the business a clear competitive moat. The $70 valuation assumes SpaceX will successfully reuse Starship’s upper stage by late 2028 and conduct several launches each week. Greater reusability could lower launch costs, strengthen Starlink’s economics and make orbital computing more practical. The analysis values SpaceX’s launch and connectivity operations at $35 per share and its cash holdings at another $7. Nvidia (NVDA) wants to reduce the time it takes for its customers to start generating revenue from its AI systems. At its GTC event in Berlin on Wednesday, the company unveiled its DSX POD, a reference design for an AI data center packed into a box about the size of a standard shipping container. Data center construction can take months, if not years, to get up and running. And because they don't start generating revenue until they begin processing AI tokens, the longer a data center takes to come online, the more expenses pile up. The DSX POD is meant to serve as a faster, modular solution for companies that need access to data center capabilities sooner rather than later. "The moment then you have to install these AI factories, and they're gigantic. And putting these AI factories into service takes months. If we could reduce that months, you know, from the moment that the systems are shipped to the moment that it's deployed and being operational, if we could reduce it from months to weeks or even a month, that will be completely game-changing for all of these AI factories," CEO Jensen Huang told Deirdre Bosa. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. According to Nvidia, the Vera Rubin-powered DSX PODs will arrive on site, ready to be plugged into the power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, reducing deployment time from six months to 14 days. The company said DSX PODs won't replace traditional data centers, but will serve as a means to start running AI applications before brick-and-mortar facilities are ready. "With Nvidia DSX POD, we're bringing factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure construction — reducing deployment time from months to weeks so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online faster," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. According to the company, the DSX POD supports liquid cooling, but because it uses dry-cooler designs, it can save up to 54 million liters of water per day versus a standard data center. Standing up data centers more quickly doesn't just help Nvidia's customers, though. Faster data center deployment should ease at least one of the chokepoints in the AI build-out, which means faster chip sales for Nvidia. Semiconductors aren't the only bottleneck for data center builders. Getting the electricity necessary to power those processors is also a concern. And power plants take far longer to construct than data centers. Nvidia said it's working with partners, including Anduril, Armada, Bull, Crusoe, Dell Technologies (DELL), Foxconn, and others, to begin delivering the DSX POD in early 2027. title: European Mobility Leaders Build Safe Vehicles and Robotaxi Fleets on NVIDIA Hyperion - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
GTC Berlin—NVIDIA today announced that leading automakers in Europe and mobility providers, including Bolt with Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles and Einride, are showcasing selected autonomous-mobility use cases on the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform, demonstrating potential applications for level 3 and level 4 vehicles as well as future robotaxi fleets. In addition, Volvo Cars is adopting Hyperion and NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack software for safe automated driving. NVIDIA also introduced new AI and safety technologies to help developers build, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles (AVs) at scale. Autonomous transportation represents a multitrillion-dollar opportunity, with robotaxis leading the move to commercial level 4 deployment. NVIDIA Hyperion and the NVIDIA Halos full-stack safety system give automakers and mobility providers the computing performance, safety foundation and long-term support to bring AVs and robotaxi fleets to market at scale. “Robotaxis are the first mass-market application of robotics and physical AI, reinventing how people and goods move,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “NVIDIA Hyperion, together with our Halos safety operating system, gives our partners a full-stack robotaxi platform designed to achieve full autonomy and the highest levels of safety, bringing us closer to a future where everything that moves is autonomous.” Mobility Leaders in Europe Build on NVIDIA Hyperion
Automakers and mobility providers in Europe are pursuing various paths to autonomy, from passenger vehicles and robotaxi fleets to autonomous freight trucks. NVIDIA Hyperion’s modular architecture supports all of these programs, compatible with NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack autonomous driving software as well as partners’ own driving software. Bolt has selected NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack for its European robotaxi program, beginning with future Lucid vehicles built on Hyperion. Bolt and NVIDIA will adapt the software for European roads and integrate it into vehicles from multiple manufacturers, combining NVIDIA’s driving and safety technologies with Bolt’s fleet-management systems, operations and local market expertise. Bolt plans to begin gathering real-world driving data to support the development and validation of the autonomous driving technology — subject to regulatory approval — in Madrid in 2027, with Germany being a priority for future deployment as part of a planned European rollout of at least 25,000 level 4-capable future Lucid vehicles built on NVIDIA Hyperion. At GTC Berlin, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is presenting its autonomous ID. Buzz AD vehicle platform with Hyperion to support multiple autonomous-driving systems. Hyperion provides a common computing and sensor architecture designed to simplify integration and validation, helping developers and mobility operators bring robotaxi and commercial transport services to market. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with Hyperion, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Mercedes-Benz is extending its partnership with NVIDIA on Hyperion and Alpamayo Stack to support the development of the automaker’s L3 and L4 capabilities. The company also announced that MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO, developed in partnership with NVIDIA, will soon get approval for urban point-to-point urban driver assistance in Germany, helping drivers navigate journeys through complex city traffic. Beyond passenger vehicles and robotaxis, Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using Halos, Alpamayo and NVIDIA Cosmos™ open world models to develop and validate its driving system, while TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich plan to integrate Hyperion to develop and validate systems for autonomous public transportation in Germany. NVIDIA technology and manufacturing partners are also helping expand the AV ecosystem, with Aptiv, Valeo and Schaeffler building Hyperion-based computing platforms that can be integrated by vehicle manufacturers for L4 AVs and robotaxis. Scaling Safe Autonomy With NVIDIA Halos
Halos provides the safety foundation for NVIDIA’s AV platform, bringing together AI computing, safety software and validation from development through deployment. To give developers repeatable ways to evaluate driving behavior and simulation accuracy, NVIDIA today introduced Halos SAFE — the Safety Assurance Framework for Evaluation — with dSPACE, IVEX and TÜV Rheinland collaborating on evaluation workflows. Halos SAFE connects simulation, software- and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, on-road testing and fleet monitoring through defined scenarios, tests and measurable performance criteria to generate traceable safety evidence that supports deployment. The Halos SAFE ecosystem also includes JLR, Mercedes-Benz, Volvo Cars, 51Sim, aiMotive, AVL, Deepen AI, Foretellix and Synopsys. Accelerating AV Development
Developing AVs means teaching AI to handle the diversity of real-world driving, then bringing that intelligence into the vehicle. NVIDIA’s latest models, tools and blueprints help developers prepare driving data, improve models and evaluate performance: Uber and NVIDIA are developing a data factory powered by Cosmos to curate and process data for AV development. The effort is part of a broader partnership spanning AI development infrastructure, Hyperion-based vehicles and Uber’s global ride-hailing network. Porsche is leading the development of a data flywheel workflow across Volkswagen Group brands through Voxel51, using NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory and Omniverse NuRec on Microsoft Azure to turn fleet data into datasets and simulations for evaluating autonomous-driving models. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle duration by up to 85%. Watch the GTC Berlin keynote from Huang and explore sessions. About NVIDIA

title: Micron and Nvidia Are the 2 Biggest Drivers of S&P 500 Earnings Growth. Are Their Stocks Buys? - The Motley Fool
content: Take out two chipmakers, and the index's third-quarter earnings growth rate falls by almost a third. So why are both stocks far below their peaks? Two chipmakers are carrying an unusual share of the market's profit growth. In its Oct. 16 Earnings Insight report, FactSet listed Micron Technology (MU +1.96%) and Nvidia (NVDA +2.54%) as the two biggest contributors to year-over-year earnings growth for the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.58%) in the third quarter of 2026. FactSet's blended growth rate of the index, which mixes reported results with estimates for companies yet to report, is at 29%. Without Micron and Nvidia, it would drop to 20%. Said another way, two companies are providing about 9 percentage points of the growth in an index of 500. Their stocks have been moving the other way. As of this writing, Nvidia shares are around $217 and have lost 9% since their Oct. 6 record close. Micron is near $905, about 25% below its June 25 record close of $1,213.56. I think this gap between what these companies earn and what their shares cost makes both stocks worth buying today. Micron's part of FactSet's number is an actual result, not a forecast. The memory maker's fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, which ended Sept. 3 and was reported on Sept. 30, goes into FactSet's third-quarter total. Micron's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share came in at $33.42, a gain of over 1,000% from the $3.03 it earned in the year-ago period. Revenue grew 379% year over year to $54.2 billion. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Notably, the margin expansion behind that rise looks like it's mostly played out. Micron's GAAP operating margin (operating income as a share of revenue) hit 80.7% in fiscal Q4, versus 32.3% a year earlier. But that was just a little over the 80.4% it had in fiscal Q3, and management's guidance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 calls for an operating margin of around 82%. So Micron's profit growth from here depends mainly on revenue instead of far higher margins. And the company expects revenue to keep rising, to about $61.5 billion in fiscal Q1. The shares don't reflect much of that. At roughly $905, Micron trades at about 12 times the $74.33 in earnings per share it posted for fiscal 2026. This price-to-earnings ratio is under half the S&P 500's ratio of 26, based on the index's last 12 months of earnings, according to FactSet. And if Micron just matched its fiscal Q4 profit for four quarters, the stock would cost about 7 times earnings. A price this low suggests investors expect memory prices, and Micron's profits with them, to drop eventually. Memory prices have always run in cycles, so it might happen. For now, though, Micron's own outlook points higher. Nvidia is different. The artificial intelligence (AI) chip leader hasn't reported its fiscal third quarter yet, so FactSet still uses an estimate for it. Still, Nvidia's outlook for the fiscal third quarter points to around $108 billion in revenue, nearly twice the $57.0 billion it posted a year before. Nvidia's profits are growing even faster than its sales. In its fiscal 2027 second quarter, the three months ending July 26, 2026, Nvidia's non-GAAP net income jumped 118% year over year, to $54.0 billion, while revenue rose 106%. Profit also climbed 18% from the $45.5 billion Nvidia made in fiscal Q1. And the company's non-GAAP gross margin widened to 75% from 72.5% a year before, so Nvidia doesn't seem to be cutting prices to get this growth. Investors aren't paying much of a premium for it, either. On analysts' average estimate for the fiscal year ending in January 2028, the stock sells for around 14 times earnings. For a business whose profit is more than doubling, the market seems to doubt this rate can hold. Of course, an outlook isn't a result. A drop in data center budgets at the big cloud companies could slow Nvidia down fast. The ranking also says something about where this growth comes from. FactSet said that its next three contributors, Meta Platforms, EchoStar, and Boeing, are all getting help from easy comparisons, because their year-ago results had big charges. Last quarter, Micron and Nvidia placed third and fourth behind two businesses whose profits were boosted by investment gains. Micron and Nvidia reached the top this time by earning far more from their own operations. Both companies are growing profits much faster than the S&P 500, and neither stock is priced like it. Memory prices could still turn, or AI spending could slow, and either would probably hit these shares hard. title: CRWV, NBIS, NVDA Jump Overnight: Musk Says SpaceX Could Rent Compute ‘Several Times Over,’ Analyst Dismisses Glut Fears - TradingView
content: CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and major AI infrastructure stocks climbed overnight late Tuesday as SpaceX’s strong compute demand prompted analysts to challenge oversupply fears and highlight rising rental rates and a faster-than-expected capacity expansion. CRWV rose 5% and NBIS climbed 6% overnight, while Nvidia (NVDA) and ASML (ASML) each gained 2% and Intel (INTC) advanced 4%. “We are also, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute,” Musk said on the latest SpaceX earnings call. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” SpaceX has encountered the shortage itself. Musk said efforts to shift inference workloads elsewhere and free up capacity for training hit the same wall across GB300s, GB200s, TPUs, Trainiums and older H100s: no availability. He compared the search to Monty Python’s cheese-shop sketch — a shop with plenty of varieties to ask for, but no cheese to sell. “It is ridiculous. I do not think we are going to have a demand issue here,” Musk said. The strong demand outlook lifted shares of AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent GPU computing capacity to customers. SpaceX’s Compute Outlook Gives Neocloud Bulls Fresh Fodder Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said SpaceX’s Super Intelligence business beat expectations by 17%, calling the results good news for neoclouds. “This is profitable revenue and a sign that the narrative that we have oversupply of compute is off base,” he said. The segment generated $7.6 billion in third-quarter (Q3) revenue, about 52% of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion total, compared with 33% in the June quarter, Munster noted. CFO Bret Johnsen said SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially even excluding the Cursor acquisition. Munster also said investors underappreciate the business helping finance SpaceX’s connectivity and launch ambitions. “Super Intelligence business (compute) doesn't get the love it deserves from many investors because it's seen as not as sexy as the other segments,” he said. Musk said the shortage was supporting prices even for older hardware. “That is why you see things like even old computers, like the H100s, renting for more than they rented when they were new,” he said. SpaceX favors short contracts at effectively spot-market rates, betting that better AI software will increase the value generated from its compute. “We see them renewing at higher dollars per watt, not lower dollars per watt,” Musk said. Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management chief futurist Brett Winton highlighted the implications for providers able to switch on capacity quickly. “Elon's commentary also suggests that renewals on the same chips are increasing year over year,” he said. “This is bullish for anyone that can actually attach a gpu to power in as little a time as possible.” Johnsen said pricing was slightly above the high end of the previously discussed $30 to $30-per-watt range, with new deployments paying back in less than a year. Winton said contracts tracking above $50 billion per gigawatt exceeded ARK’s model, while noting potential customer concentration. Musk suggested returns could improve further: “I am not saying this will happen; it is not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year.” SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity and expects 2.5 to 3 GW by year-end. Musk expressed high confidence in adding another 10 GW during 2027. “I would be surprised if we brought on less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year,” he said. This exceeds ARK’s forecast of slightly less than 8 GW, Winton said. Reaching 3 GW this year would also surpass its 2.1-GW expectation, he noted. “This is quite positive,” Winton said. “At the margin I was somewhat expecting cautionary commentary on GWs delivered given on-the-ground complications.” Musk also outlined an aim for 20 GW of additional power and cooling infrastructure next year, while presenting more than 20 GW of active compute in 2027 as a smaller possibility. Winton separately said reaching 20 GW of compute by the end of 2028 could offer a credible catch-up path to frontier AI competitors; ARK had expected that milestone around early 2030. The expansion comes after $19.6 billion of capital spending in Q3. Munster said the plans suggested 2027 spending above the Street’s $162 billion expectation. Niles Investment Management founder Dan Niles pointed to SpaceX’s earnings beat and aggressive spending outlook as reasons for growing confidence in a near-term AI rebound. “My conviction of a near-term AI rally continues to grow,” he said on X. SpaceX forecast first-quarter revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion and fourth-quarter capital spending of $35 billion to $40 billion. Niles put those outlooks 57% and nearly 90% above consensus, respectively. He argued that the AI infrastructure trade looked oversold even while acknowledging neocloud funding challenges, slowing revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic, and bipartisan opposition to data centers. “Maybe the SpaceX earnings and Super Micro positive pre-announcement [preliminary q1 sales update] today are the trigger to start the next AI related rally regardless of whether we have seen THE TOP or not.” Musk said SpaceX was tracking to bring 200,000 Nvidia GB300s online monthly through year-end, with next year’s deployments increasingly focused on Vera Rubin. A training cluster would contain 440,000 Vera Rubin computers by the end of Q2 2027. Winton said that SpaceX’s ability to power and deploy chips quickly makes it a more reliable Nvidia customer. Musk identified power, cooling and infrastructure as bigger constraints than chips. Intel and ASML connect through Terafab. Intel is a strategic partner in the project, which Musk said aims for a functional test chip around May or June 2027 and volume production in the second half of 2028. “Now, these are very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome,” Musk said, while cautioning that the schedule carried substantial uncertainty. Musk said Grok Bot could eventually use most of SpaceX’s compute, adding another source of demand alongside external customers. “I've never seen anything grow this fast,” he said. President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said Grok Bot had hit 800,000 paid weekly users earlier this month, more than doubling over the previous month. Munster projected 50 million daily users within six months, versus his estimate of 5 million currently. Musk linked the expansion to potential annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Winton said the upper end represented upside from monetizing Grok Bot rather than simply renting infrastructure. “You don't need to make wild assumptions about AI software monetization in order to make that ARR forecast work,” he said. ASML’s sentiment was ‘neutral’, also amid ‘normal’ message volume. INTC leads the group with a 148% gain so far this year, followed by NBIS at 105%, ASML at 53% and NVDA at 16%, while CRWV has fallen 13%. title: Nvidia Reportedly Just Landed $35 Billion In Chip Orders From Chinese Companies. Here's Why That Could Be Great News for the Stock - The Motley Fool
content: The company has sold hardly any chips to China since early last year, due to government restrictions. It has not been an easy couple of weeks for the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia (NVDA +2.54%), whose stock has fallen by over 9%. AI concerns have been front and center, as Anthropic appears to be dragging its feet on its suspected initial public offering, and as investors fret about some of the balance sheets of debt-laden neoclouds. Nvidia is still having a solid year, but the company has posted incredibly strong results in its first two quarterly reports and arguably hasn't been rewarded as much as some investors would have expected. Earlier today, Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Chinese companies, including ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent, have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia Blackwell chips, collectively worth $35 billion. After the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on China in 2025, it told Nvidia in April of that year that it would need to obtain an export license to continue selling data center chips to Chinese companies. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $3,105,454*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. This had also been an issue in former President Joe Biden's administration, with both administrations citing national security concerns. However, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, met with Trump on several occasions and also lobbied Washington regulators, eventually striking a deal in which Nvidia would cede 15% of its Chinese chip sales to the government. Most of those reports came last year, and there hasn't been much of an update since. Still, due to reservations from both U.S. and Chinese regulators, sales have hardly resumed. Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress said on the company's most recent earnings call at the end of August that less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue came from customers in China, and it was for Nvidia's older-generation Hopper 200 chips. Kress also said that Hopper sales are dilutive to gross margins, so it's positive that the company is able to sell Blackwell chips to Chinese customers. The even better news for investors is that Nvidia has been providing forward guidance without including potential sales to Chinese companies. On the last quarterly call, Kress said the company is projecting revenue for the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027 to come in around $108 billion, so $35 billion is not an insignificant number. However, Reuters also reported that Nvidia may not be able to fulfill all Chinese orders because it had not planned for such production levels. One source told Reuters that Nvidia may only be able to fill 5% to 10% of orders and has capacity to produce at most 3 million Blackwell chips globally in 2027. Investors and analysts will clearly be anxious to learn more about the Chinese orders on the company's next earnings call, including the magnitude of the orders, how much the company can fill, and how much of the sales it must cede to the government. Despite the news, Nvidia's stock only traded marginally higher as of 2:04 p.m. ET today, and the market was broadly in the green. The stock has had some difficulty gaining traction, despite reporting blowout numbers and guidance each quarter so far this year. Part of it likely has to do with Nvidia's roughly $5.2 trillion market cap and the fact that it's already guiding for 70% revenue growth in its fiscal year 2028. Investors are also nervous about the AI trade and whether companies can keep buying chips at the same level they have been. Still, it's hard to view the demand in China as anything but broadly good news for Nvidia and the AI trade on the whole. title: Amazon (AMZN) is buying billions in Nvidia (NVDA) AI systems it can't yet turn on, Business Insider reports - Newsquawk
content: Deliveries of this kind, hardware arriving ahead of the power and cooling capacity needed to run it, have been a recurring feature of the AI buildout cycle, and the distinction that matters is between a supply bottleneck and a deployment bottleneck: the former constrains the chipmaker, the latter the hyperscaler, and the market has historically read them differently. For NVDA, racks shipped into staging count as recognized revenue at the point of delivery, so a buyer sitting on unpowered inventory flatters near-term shipments while raising the question of how much backlog is real end-demand versus capacity parked ahead of energization. For AMZN, the read runs through capex versus utilization: prior episodes where cloud operators absorbed hardware faster than facilities could be commissioned have eventually shown up as depreciation running ahead of AWS revenue, a gap the equity has historically punished when disclosed. The figures here come from internal correspondence cited by a single outlet, so confirmation sits with the next quarterly prints on both sides, specifically NVDA's shipments commentary and AMZN's capex and cloud capacity language. Worth noting that staged delivery before final deployment is also standard practice for large data center programs, so the telling detail is the scale relative to energization timelines rather than the existence of the staging itself. title: NYSE American Options launches extended trading hours for SPY, NVDA and peers - InvestmentNews
content:
NYSE American Options has introduced pre- and post-market trading sessions for a select group of equity options, expanding access for advisors and their clients beyond the standard trading day. The New York Stock Exchange, part of Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), launched NYSE American Options Extended Trading Hours (ETH) on October 20, 2026, giving market participants additional access to options listed on NYSE American. The initial group of eligible symbols includes options overlying key macroeconomic-focused ETFs (SPY, IWM, and GLD) alongside options on large-cap technology names including Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon, and Oracle. The early trading session runs from 7:30 AM to 9:25 AM ET, while the late trading session operates from 4:00 PM to 4:15 PM ET. The launch positions NYSE American in a fast-moving race among major exchanges to extend options access. Cboe Global Markets received SEC approval in May 2026 to offer extended trading hours for select multi-listed equity options on the Cboe Options Exchange, with that offering beginning July 13, 2026. NYSE American said that investor demand to trade options outside regular hours was growing, that non-U.S. investors found it difficult to participate when options traded only during the standard U.S. session, and that U.S. investors trading stocks after hours could not access the options market to hedge their positions. For advisors using options strategies to manage client risk particularly around earnings events or macro data releases, the expanded window provides a longer runway to respond to overnight news before the core session opens. Extended hours trading will be limited to up to 100 multiply-listed equity option classes meeting specific eligibility criteria, including average daily options volume of 150,000 contracts, underlying equity market capitalization of $50 billion, and underlying equity average daily trading volume of 10 million shares. Kevin Tyrrell, Chief Product Officer at NYSE, said the move "reflects market demand for investment opportunities and reliable risk management during a longer period of time," adding that the exchange plans to bring a similar approach to equities in December 2026. Brokers are also required to disclose specific risks to clients before accepting orders for extended-hours execution. Required disclosures must cover material trading risks such as lower liquidity, higher volatility, changing prices, exaggerated effects from news announcements, and wider bid-ask spreads. The NYSE move also signals a broader structural shift in market infrastructure. Five symbols (GLD, IWM, QQQ, SPY, and XLF) already traded until 4:15 PM ET under existing rules, with this launch now formalizing and expanding those sessions alongside the new pre-market window. For more details on eligible symbols and session rules, the NYSE American Options Extended Trading Hours Fact Sheet is available via ICE's public documents portal. title: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments - CNBC
content:
Nvidia is increasing its investments in Europe’s artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI. The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker’s nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday. The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments. Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites. The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors. Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country’s economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany’s small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data,” Merz said. “This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz’s remarks while highlighting Germany’s expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country’s industrial capabilities. “AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability,” Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses. Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications. Earlier in the day, Siemens had also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%. Huang had also visited France last week, where he announced investments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development.
